verdicts.trueWording: "Written on the Dark is equally as impressive for its accessibility and its density"
verdicts.note: Globe and Mail page fetched raw (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200). Sentence present word for word in the penultimate body paragraph, which continues "qualities that may seem to be at odds, but aren't." Byline David Moscrop, published June 6, 2025. Claim's 'equally impressive' drops only the source's 'as'.

verdicts.trueWording: "It's not giving away much to open this review with the closing words"
verdicts.note: Raw page: the review's first body line is the quoted closing words, immediately followed by "It's not giving away much to open this review with the closing words of Written on the Dark, Guy Gavriel Kay's tale of a tavern poet...". Both limbs (opens; cites the closing words) supported.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'a four-word sentence' — the sentence Moscrop quotes, "I did that.", is three words
verdicts.trueWording: "I did that. I did that." — a three-word sentence repeated once
verdicts.note: The quotation is on the raw page verbatim, as the review's opening line, and 'repeated once' is right. The word count is not: I/did/that is three words, so the page's own text refutes the 'four-word' limb. Everything else in the claim holds.

verdicts.trueWording: "even for the mysteries it refuses to explain, it makes sense"
verdicts.note: Raw page, paragraph beginning "The brilliance of Written on the Dark": "Maybe that's the least realistic thing about this novel of fantasy, that even for the mysteries it refuses to explain, it makes sense." Quote verbatim; both limbs (makes sense; mysteries it refuses to explain) supported.

verdicts.trueWording: "A master of telling small stories in a big world, Kay reveals spots of hope"
verdicts.note: BookPage page fetched raw (HTTP 200). Final review paragraph opens with the phrase word for word. Page also carries the 'STARRED REVIEW' flag, the May 17, 2022 date and 'Review by Noah Fram', so the attribution limbs hold too.

verdicts.trueWording: "his characters see their homes fade from the map and their own lives taken for the pettiest of causes"
verdicts.note: First body paragraph of the raw BookPage review: "Kay's fictional worlds, while beautiful, are defined by this bleak inertia; his characters see their homes fade from the map and their own lives taken for the pettiest of causes." Quote verbatim; the claim's 'their lives' merely drops the source's 'own'.

verdicts.trueWording: "That means he doesn't have to play by the more restrictive rules of modern publishing"
verdicts.note: Christianity Today page fetched raw (HTTP 200), paragraph beginning "It helps that Kay, 70, has been writing successfully for decades." The rule list, attributed with 'he told me', opens "Rules like: Don't jump from the past tense to the present tense." Seniority limb (age 70, decades of success) and the freedom limb both on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: "Don't hop between characters' heads—just choose one perspective per chapter"
verdicts.note: Same raw CT paragraph: "Don't hop between characters' heads—just choose one perspective per chapter or, ideally, one perspective for the entire book." Listed among the rules Kay told the reporter he need not play by, so the 'does not have to obey' limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: "don't write an entire chapter from the viewpoint of a grizzled medieval courier who is largely irrelevant to the plot"
verdicts.note: Raw CT page, closing item of the same rule list: "And definitely don't write an entire chapter from the viewpoint of a grizzled medieval courier who is largely irrelevant to the plot." Quote verbatim; the 'plot-irrelevant' limb is the page's own 'largely irrelevant to the plot'.

verdicts.trueWording: "'I trust my readers,' he said simply."
verdicts.note: Raw CT page, immediately after the one-line paragraph "Still, Kay has resisted.": "'I trust my readers,' he said simply. 'And at this stage, my readers—and I mean it when I say this is a gift—my readers let me get away with it.'" The claim's 'simply' is the page's own adverb.

verdicts.trueWording: "Every book I've ever written has been, in part, an attempt to look at how different the past is and how similar it is"
verdicts.note: Raw CT page, direct quotation attributed to Kay ('Kay said'), from the Toronto interview described earlier in the piece. Quote verbatim; 'every book', 'in part' and the different/similar pairing all present.

verdicts.trueWording: "wanted security, wanted a roof, wanted a harvest"
verdicts.note: Raw CT page, same Kay quotation continuing: "The people of the past are strange and alien and wildly different from us, but they also loved their children, loved their spouses, didn't love their spouses, wanted security, wanted a roof, wanted a harvest." All three concrete wants verbatim and in order.

verdicts.trueWording: "There are no elaborate, concrete magic systems here; instead, the books are haunted by the other, the transcendent, and mystery"
verdicts.note: Raw CT page, paragraph beginning "Kay's characteristic 'quarter turn to the fantastic'". Quote verbatim and the 'haunted by the transcendent' limb is the page's own clause (which also names 'the other' and 'mystery'). Reporter's own sentence, as the claim's attribution says.

verdicts.trueWording: "When we work with distant history, to a very great degree, we are all guessing."
verdicts.note: BrightWeavings 'Home and Away' fetched raw (HTTP 200); page header confirms the amended-speech provenance and the shorter Globe and Mail version of fall 1999. Sentence sits in the paragraph following the Rodrigo Diaz / El Cid passage; the next clause extends it to 'those who claim to be factual historians as it is of novelists', so the claim's 'writers' is inside the source's scope. Claim's 'to a great degree' drops the source's 'very'.

verdicts.trueWording: "by inventing the setting and inventing a man based on Rodrigo Diaz... I might also be demonstrating a measure of appropriate distance"
verdicts.note: Raw BrightWeavings page, El Cid paragraph, verbatim. Every limb present (invented setting; man based on Rodrigo Diaz 'but clearly not him'; appropriate distance). One softening worth flagging: Kay writes the hedged 'I might also be demonstrating', not a flat 'demonstrates', and speaks of his own book rather than as a general rule.
